title: Neonatal care: thermoregulation, jaundice and hypoglycaemia
blurb: Keep a newborn warm, act on jaundice by age in hours using NICE CG98, and manage low blood glucose using the BAPM framework.
question: Baby Zainab, born at 39 weeks, is 18 hours old. Her mother notices her skin looks yellow. What is the most appropriate action?

teach.body: In the first days of life babies are poor at keeping warm, clearing bilirubin and keeping blood glucose steady. Formally, these are thermoregulation, neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia (jaundice) and neonatal hypoglycaemia, each with national guidance: NICE CG98 for jaundice and the BAPM framework for hypoglycaemia. Plain English: keep the baby warm, look for yellow skin in good light, and check glucose in babies at risk, because each problem can harm the brain if missed.
teach.cite: NICE CG98 (updated 2023); BAPM hypoglycaemia framework (Jan 2024, corrected Sep 2024)

teach.caption: Dry the baby, use a hat, give skin-to-skin, avoid draughts and cold surfaces, keep the room warm.

teach.body: After birth, NICE advises skin-to-skin contact as soon as possible and keeping the baby warm and dry. A temperature under 36°C, or 38°C or more, is a red flag in a newborn (NICE NG194). A cold baby burns glucose and oxygen to make heat, so cold stress and hypoglycaemia often go together. First response to a mildly cool, well baby: skin-to-skin with the parent, a hat and a warm, draught-free room, then recheck.

items.label: Measure bilirubin within 6 h if suspected

teach.caption: Jaundice in the first 24 hours: serum bilirubin within 2 hours and urgent medical review within 6 hours.

teach.note: Prolonged jaundice: ask about pale chalky stools and dark urine, and measure conjugated bilirubin (biliary atresia must not be missed).

bands.label: More than two, no signs: treat

teach.caption: Values in mmol/L. Check at-risk babies' first glucose before the second feed (2–4 hours after birth).

teach.h: Caring for a baby at risk of low glucose
items: Identify risk: maternal diabetes, preterm, growth restricted, maternal beta-blockers (for example labetalol).
Keep warm and feed early; feeds no more than 3 hours apart.
First glucose before the second feed, 2 to 4 hours after birth.
Watch for abnormal signs such as abnormal feeding behaviour, lethargy, floppiness, apnoea or seizures (jitteriness alone is not a sign).
At-risk babies stay in hospital for at least 24 hours.

teach.text: Read the BAPM threshold exactly: an at-risk baby without signs needs treatment after MORE THAN TWO measurements below 2.0 mmol/L, not after 'two consecutive' values. A single value under 1.0, or under 2.5 with abnormal signs, needs treatment at once.

teach.h: Scenario: Baby Isaac on the postnatal ward
teach.body: Isaac was born at 38 weeks. His mother took labetalol in pregnancy. Nurse Rhiannon recognises maternal beta-blockers as a risk factor. She keeps Isaac skin-to-skin with a hat on, supports an early breastfeed and plans his first glucose check before the second feed. At 3 hours his pre-feed glucose is 1.6 mmol/L and he has no abnormal signs: she gives 40% glucose gel 200 mg/kg, supports a feed and rechecks before the next feed.

items: Newborn temperature under 36°C or 38°C or more is a red flag.
Visible jaundice under 24 hours: serum bilirubin within 2 hours.
No icterometers and no sunlight; check sclerae and gums on darker skin.
Prolonged jaundice: over 14 days (term) or 21 days (preterm); ask about pale stools.
Glucose: under 1.0 any time, or under 2.5 with signs, treat; gel 200 mg/kg for 1.0–1.9.

summary: You can now prevent and correct cold stress in a newborn and act on jaundice by the baby's age in hours using CG98. You can also identify babies at risk of hypoglycaemia and apply the current BAPM treatment thresholds.

A.q: Baby Zainab, born at 39 weeks, is 18 hours old. Her mother notices her skin looks yellow. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Measure serum bilirubin within 2 hours
Use a transcutaneous meter and recheck tomorrow
Advise placing her near a sunny window
Increase feeds and review at 24 hours
A.why: CG98: jaundice in the first 24 hours is pathological until proved otherwise. Measure serum bilirubin urgently (within 2 hours) and arrange urgent medical review.

whyNot.1: Transcutaneous meters are for babies over 24 hours old; under 24 hours a serum level is needed urgently.
whyNot.2: Sunlight is not a treatment for neonatal jaundice.
whyNot.3: Waiting delays urgent assessment of early jaundice.

A.q: Baby Grace, born at term, is 2 days old on the children's ward. Her axillary temperature is 36.0°C. She is alert, pink and feeding well. What is the most appropriate first action?
options: Place her in an incubator at 37°C
Skin-to-skin with her mother in a warm room
Bathe her in warm water
Give an extra formula feed
A.why: For a mildly cool but well baby, skin-to-skin with a parent, a hat and a warm, draught-free room are the first steps, followed by a recheck.

whyNot.0: An incubator is not the first step for a well, mildly cool term baby.
whyNot.3: Feeding helps glucose but does not address heat loss first.

A.q: Which baby has a recognised risk factor that means blood glucose monitoring should be planned?
options: Term baby born by caesarean
Term baby whose mother took labetalol
Term baby with a cephalhaematoma
Term baby of a mother with asthma
A.why: Maternal beta-blockers such as labetalol are a recognised risk factor for neonatal hypoglycaemia (BAPM).

whyNot.0: Caesarean birth in a term baby is not by itself a BAPM risk factor.
whyNot.2: A cephalhaematoma is not a listed risk factor for hypoglycaemia.
whyNot.3: Maternal asthma is not a listed risk factor.

B.q: Leo, born at 40 weeks, is 16 days old, breastfed and still jaundiced. His mother says his stools have become pale. What should the nurse do?
options: Reassure that breastfeeding jaundice lasts weeks
Advise switching to formula
Arrange a check of conjugated bilirubin
Start phototherapy at home
B.why: Jaundice over 14 days in a term baby is prolonged. Pale chalky stools suggest conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia (such as biliary atresia): measure conjugated bilirubin.

whyNot.0: Pale stools are a warning sign that must not be put down to breastfeeding.
whyNot.1: Breastfeeding usually continues; stopping it does not investigate the cause.
whyNot.3: Phototherapy does not treat conjugated jaundice and would delay diagnosis.

B.q: Kofi, 3 days old, has dark brown skin. The nurse is checking him for jaundice in a dim ward. Which approach is best?
options: Check his sclerae and gums in bright light
Press an icterometer against his nose
Judge his level from skin colour
Wait until his skin looks yellow
B.why: CG98: examine the naked baby in bright, ideally natural light, checking the sclerae, gums and blanched skin, as jaundice is harder to see on darker skin.

whyNot.2: Visual inspection should not be used to estimate the bilirubin level.
whyNot.3: Skin yellowing is harder to see on darker skin, so waiting risks missing jaundice.

B.q: Baby Mia, born at 39 weeks to a mother with gestational diabetes, is 3 hours old. Her pre-feed glucose is 1.5 mmol/L. She is feeding and has no abnormal signs. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Recheck in 6 hours
Start IV glucose at once
Give 40% glucose gel and feed
Give 10 mL of water
B.why: BAPM: a reading of 1.0 to 1.9 mmol/L without abnormal signs is managed with 40% glucose gel 200 mg/kg plus a feed, then a recheck before the next feed.

whyNot.0: Waiting 6 hours is too long; feeds and checks should be no more than 3 hours apart.
whyNot.1: IV glucose is for values under 1.0, abnormal signs or failed gel and feeding.
whyNot.3: Water does not raise blood glucose.

C.q: Baby Ruby, born at term to a mother with type 1 diabetes, is 4 hours old. She is lethargic and feeding poorly, and her glucose is 2.2 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Record it and recheck before the next feed
Treat as a value needing action and get urgent review
Give gel and wait for two more readings
Reassure as the value is above 2.0
C.why: BAPM: a single value under 2.5 mmol/L with abnormal clinical signs (lethargy, abnormal feeding behaviour) needs treatment and urgent medical review.

whyNot.0: Abnormal signs with a value under 2.5 need action now.
whyNot.2: The 'more than two values under 2.0' rule is for babies without signs.
whyNot.3: The 2.0 threshold applies to babies without signs; with signs the threshold is 2.5.

C.q: Ellie is 20 hours old and having phototherapy. She is breastfed. Her mother asks whether she can stop to feed and whether Ellie needs extra water. What should the nurse advise?
options: Feed breaks up to 30 minutes; no extra water
No breaks until bilirubin falls; add water
Switch to formula during treatment
Feed breaks of 2 hours; give extra water
C.why: CG98: during phototherapy give breaks of up to 30 minutes for breastfeeding, and do not routinely give extra fluids to breastfed babies.

whyNot.1: Short feeding breaks are encouraged, and extra water is not routinely given.
whyNot.3: Breaks are up to 30 minutes, and extra water is not routine.

C.q: Baby Ola is at risk of hypoglycaemia (growth restricted). He has no abnormal signs. His pre-feed readings have been 1.9, 2.3, 1.8 and 1.9 mmol/L. What does the BAPM framework indicate?
options: Continue routine feeds; values are acceptable
Treat, as more than two readings are below 2.0
Treat if the next value is under 1.0
Stop monitoring as he has no signs
C.why: BAPM framework (2024) practice point 6: in an at-risk baby without signs, more than two measurements below 2.0 mmol/L need treatment. Ola has three.

whyNot.0: Three readings below 2.0 cross the treatment threshold.
whyNot.2: Treatment is indicated now; under 1.0 is a separate urgent threshold.
whyNot.3: At-risk babies continue monitoring for at least 24 hours.

reteach.title: Warm, yellow, sweet
reteach.question: What are the three numbers you must not forget in a newborn?

blocks.body: Warm: under 36°C is a red flag; skin-to-skin, hat, warm room. Yellow: jaundice before 24 hours means serum bilirubin within 2 hours. Sweet: glucose under 1.0 any time, or under 2.5 with signs, needs treatment; more than two values under 2.0 in a well at-risk baby also needs treatment.

blocks.text: Gel is not for every low reading. A value under 1.0 mmol/L, or any low value with abnormal signs, needs urgent medical treatment, not just gel and a feed.

explain.body: Newborns lose heat by evaporation (wet skin), conduction (cold surfaces), convection (draughts) and radiation (to cold walls and windows). Prevent each one: dry, warm surfaces, no draughts, away from cold windows, skin-to-skin and a hat.

test.q: A newborn is placed on cold scales without a cover. Which route of heat loss is this?
options: Evaporation
Convection
Radiation
Conduction
test.why: Direct contact with a cold surface causes heat loss by conduction.

whyNot.0: Evaporation is heat loss from wet skin.
whyNot.1: Convection is heat loss to moving air.
whyNot.2: Radiation is heat loss to cooler surfaces not in contact.

explain.body: Visible jaundice in the first 24 hours is pathological until proved otherwise: serum bilirubin within 2 hours and urgent medical review within 6 hours. After 24 hours, measure within 6 hours if jaundice is suspected, using a TcB meter from 35 weeks.

test.q: Baby Amir is 36 hours old, born at 38 weeks, and looks jaundiced. How should his bilirubin be measured first?
options: Transcutaneous bilirubinometer
Visual estimate in daylight
Icterometer
Urine bilirubin dipstick
test.why: CG98: babies of 35 weeks or more and over 24 hours old can have bilirubin measured with a transcutaneous bilirubinometer (serum if over 250 micromol/L).

whyNot.1: Visual inspection should not be used to estimate the level.
whyNot.3: A urine dipstick does not measure serum bilirubin.

explain.body: Prolonged jaundice is over 14 days in babies born at 37 weeks or more, or over 21 days if born earlier. Look for pale chalky stools and dark urine, and measure conjugated bilirubin. Breastfeeding usually continues.

test.q: Baby Lily was born at 34 weeks and is 18 days old with visible jaundice. How should this be classed?
options: Prolonged, as it is over 14 days
Not yet prolonged for her gestation
Pathological, as she is preterm
Physiological, needing no further checks
test.why: For babies born before 37 weeks, jaundice is prolonged after 21 days, so at 18 days it is not yet prolonged, though she still needs clinical assessment.

whyNot.0: The 14-day cut-off is for babies born at 37 weeks or more.
whyNot.2: Prematurity alone does not make jaundice pathological.
whyNot.3: Visible jaundice still needs assessment and measurement.

explain.body: BAPM (Jan 2024, corrected Sept 2024): treat under 1.0 mmol/L at any time, a single value under 2.5 with abnormal signs, or more than two values under 2.0 in an at-risk baby without signs. 40% gel 200 mg/kg for readings of 1.0 to 1.9.

test.q: When should the first blood glucose be checked in a baby at risk of hypoglycaemia?
options: Immediately after birth
At 12 hours of age
At 30 minutes of age
Before the second feed
test.why: BAPM: the first glucose is measured before the second feed, 2 to 4 hours after birth.

whyNot.0: Glucose falls naturally just after birth; testing immediately is not recommended.
whyNot.1: 12 hours is far too late for an at-risk baby.
whyNot.2: 30 minutes is too early; the first check is before the second feed.
